After his speech, Trump gathered with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the General Assembly to sign a new security agreement.
The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to “take over” Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary. Trump said Tuesday the U.S. will immediately begin the process of developing a larger military presence in Greenland including “building two very major military bases.”
Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark’s territory.
Trump also held talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He’s expected to hold a more informal meeting on Tuesday evening with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez, according to the White House.
Trump also took part in an event on the Shield of Americas, an initiative Trump launched with Latin American countries earlier this year focused on combatting violent cartels.
Iran war looms large at General Assembly
The visit to the U.N. comes as Trump’s foreign policy approach — particularly his decision to start a war with Iran — has become a drag on his fellow Republicans’ hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections. Nevertheless, Trump made the case in his speech that the world is better off for his leadership.
“I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day,” Trump said.
In last year’s address at the U.N., Trump claimed the U.S. had “demolished” Iran’s nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities.
He returned to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran.
The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran’s top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles.
The energy market continues to be spooked by the war and oil prices remain elevated. Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane.
Trump’s frustration with Russia-Ukraine war mounts
In his address, the president also touched on Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine during his U.N. address — a conflict that during his 2024 campaign he predicted would be resolved on Day One of his second term. He once again expressed hope that the conflict will soon be resolved.
Trump hasn’t obscured that his patience is being tested by Ukraine’s targeting of Russia’s diesel refineries — an issue that’s added to the global oil markets’ volatility — and Russia’s targeting of Ukraine’s energy grid.
Trump last week asserted that he got the two sides to agree to not target each other’s energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy had said he was willing to go along with Trump’s plan if Russia abided by it. Russia said it could only go along with Trump’s energy truce proposal if Western energy sanctions on Moscow were lifted first.
The two sides have continued carrying out strikes on refineries and other energy infrastructure.
Trump noted that last week he signed a new sanctions bill targeting Moscow. It empowers him to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas.
The legislation includes an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Trump, however, has yet to enact the stiff penalties.
“If necessary, I will have to use them,” Trump said. “It’s time to stop the killing.”
Associated Press Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee contributed to this story.

sources.news_title: ‘Drive them into hell’: Trump ponders destruction of Iran at United Nations
sources.text:
‘Drive them into hell’: Trump ponders destruction of Iran at United Nations
French President Emmanuel Macron speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters in New York City on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump faces a “big decision” to make a deal with Iran or “annihilate” the country, he told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.
During a 37-minute speech to his international counterparts including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York City, Trump asked, “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?
“Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly … Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said.
Speaking at the annual gathering aimed at promoting multilateral discussion among 193 member nations, Trump suggested Iranian leaders were waiting to see the results of the approaching midterm elections for control of Congress before any major negotiating decision.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” he said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running.”
Iran tied to GOP midterm woes
Republicans running to maintain the majority in Congress in November face a difficult task amid sinking public support for Trump’s costly, months-long war in Iran.
The Pentagon has confirmed 19 U.S. troops have died in the conflict, though The Washington Post has reported a more accurate count is either 22 or 23. Roughly 830 service members have been injured.
And the war has spiked the price of fuel to record levels.
Trump’s approval rating hit a record low of 32%, according to the latest polling figures published Monday by Reuters/Ipsos.
Diesel hit a new high Tuesday, reaching a national average of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA. Gasoline hovered at $4.47 a gallon.
The cost of energy commodities and services, a main driver of current inflation, is up 16.3% over last year, according to the latest U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer price index.
Iran maintains its stranglehold of the Strait of Hormuz, a major global petroleum trade passageway, amid a U.S. naval blockade. And Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are now targeting the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for Saudi Arabian oil exports.
The U.S. Senate is expected to vote on yet another War Powers Resolution this week aimed at curbing Trump’s military actions in Iran. Seven House Republicans joined Democrats Sept. 16 in passing a measure to stop Trump’s unilateral decision-making in Iran.
‘They want to talk’
Trump told reporters just before 2 p.m. Eastern that U.S. officials had met with Iranian leaders after his speech for what he described as “a very good meeting.” He did not provide further detail, according to reporters who traveled with him to New York City.
Speaking to reporters just before 1 p.m. Eastern, Trump said he believed “a settlement is going to be reached.”
“They want to talk to us,” Trump said. “They have been talking to us even today. They’ve been talking to us. The relationship is developing, I’d say. But we can’t let them (have a nuclear weapon). They understand that. … And there’s a price to pay for that.”
White House pool
Trump’s trip to New York City also comes as major U.S. media organizations refused to distribute video, audio or photos of the president after he banned CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. The three organizations have sued on First Amendment grounds.
He told reporters Tuesday he has a right “to clean out fake news,” which he also described as “dangerous.”
When pressed by a reporter on how the media outlets are “dangerous,” Trump responded: “When they make statements about the war, when they make false statements, false stories, and they don’t have sources but they say they do, it’s very dangerous for our country.”
Iran’s Permanent Mission to the UN did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment. An email address listed for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs appeared to be inoperable.
Upon arrival at the United Nations this week, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araqchi criticized what he called a “cowardly” war launched by the U.S. in conjunction with Israel on Feb. 28, according to a translation posted on his ministry’s website.
“This year, after the war that took place, it is natural that this rostrum will be a place to express the oppression of the Iranian people, the martyrs of Iran, the martyrs of Minab School, and at the head of them, our martyred leader and leader,” Abbas Araqchi said, referring to early strikes during the war that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his family members and over 100 elementary school children.
Iranian security forces killed thousands of Iranians in January as part of a crackdown on protests against the current government, according to Human Rights Watch and other advocates and observers.
Threat repeated
Trump’s speech Tuesday was not the first time he’s threatened a choice between striking peace with or heavily attacking Iran.
Just before a short-lived ceasefire between Iran and the U.S. took effect in April, Trump threatened “a whole civilization will die” if Iran did not cooperate with U.S. demands.
The comment drummed up vocal opposition from some Republicans.
Speaking about another military conflict, Trump said his Board of Peace was working to stabilize the Palestinian territory of the Gaza Strip following three years of bombardment by the Israeli government. When listing the countries involved in that effort, he twice mispronounced Kazakhstan.
The board claimed in a statement in July it reached an agreement for the “COMPLETE DISARMAMENT” of Hamas, the militant organization that attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, though the conflict remains ongoing.
Trump highlighted in his Tuesday remarks to global leaders the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, and claimed the U.S. “is stronger today than ever before.” He repeated familiar refrains on domestic policies, including his immigration agenda and crime statistics in the nation’s capital.
He also briefly mentioned he would require federal documents to use the term “super intelligence” in place of “artificial intelligence.” Trump has ardently defended the use of AI without guardrails in recent weeks after tech leaders issued a warning to slow its development.
The White House pointed States Newsroom to Trump’s comments to the press following the speech.

sources.news_title: Trump Threatens to Annihilate Iran if It Doesn’t Capitulate, Agree to U.S. Terms
sources.text:
Trump Threatens to Annihilate Iran if It Doesn’t Capitulate, Agree to U.S. Terms
President Trump’s speech to the UN General Assembly today sounded more like a State of the Union address or an oration at a rally and less like a message to the world. It included the customary Trumpian braggadocio.
But he also used the forum to threaten war crimes against Iran once again. Iran had a choice, he said. Either capitulate or be “annihilated.”
This is at least the third time Trump has vowed to erase the country, which would mean millions of civilian deaths that in turn would be classified as a war crime.
Golden Age
Trump opened his talk with a big brag about his accomplishments, which is typical of the 47th president.
“Two and a half centuries after the cause of liberty found its home on this continent, I can report to you with pride that America is back and our country is stronger today than ever before,” Trump crowed:
Our economy is the envy of the world. Our military is the most powerful on earth. Our technology is second to none and we are leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet. America is rising.
Our nation is growing. Our power is expanding. Our country is doing better than ever before, and our future is very, very bright. Since I took office, we have created more than 1 million new private-sector jobs, and more Americans are working today by far than ever before.
Last week, it was announced that the poverty rate has reached its lowest level in American history. We lifted 1.5 million Americans out of poverty last year alone. Another record, the African American and Hispanic American poverty rates are at all-time lows. Real household incomes for Americans have soared to the highest level in history, 87,000 on average, surpassing the prior record that I set in my first term.
After a few more minutes touting his greatness as a president, Trump said that “we inherited a dark Age of America from the previous administration, and we turned it into the golden age of America.” Such is the heretofore unknown greatness of that Golden Age that “the entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit, and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America.”
Iran Must Obey or Else
Part of that Golden Age is paying an average of $4.48 for regular gas and even more for diesel and premium, but in any event Trump again said he would vaporize Iran.
Claiming that he made America “the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said the “fanatical Iranian regime has ruled by bloodshed and mass murder, spreading death and carnage and chaos across the entire Middle East and beyond” for 51 years.
“They were the bully of the Middle East, but they are the bully no more,” he claimed:
From the first day I entered the political arena, I’ve been unwavering. I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.
Trump claimed that Operation Midnight Hammer destroyed the country’s nuclear capability. But Iran “continued building a vast missile and drone stockpile that threatened the security of every American service member in the region and everyone else in the region.”
Trump said Iran built missiles that could strike Europe.
Speaking of the October 7, 2023 terror attack on Israel, Trump said “Iran’s supreme leader celebrated that massacre and called it a service to humanity” and that the regime had murdered 82,000 of its people.
“Just imagine if such a vile regime were ever empowered to carry out large scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield,” he said:
This was the reality we had to confront, a reality that far too many preferred to ignore.
Trump claimed that all of Iran’s Navy lies “at the bottom of the sea” that its air force and radar and anti-aircraft weapons are gone. “Their missiles and drone manufacturing capacity is almost gone,” as is “their economy,” he continued:
The only thing that isn’t gone is inflation, which is destroying their country and is now well over 300 percent.
Yet even after we agreed to a cease fire for nuclear discussions, Iran promptly violated it with brazen acts of terrorism against civilian ships from other countries.
I want to thank the UN Security Council for voting overwhelmingly to pass a resolution condemning Iran’s despicable terrorist attacks on commercial shipping.
Trump said the U.S. Navy has escorted 1 billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. “More oil is flowing than at any point since the start of the war,” he said.
“But I have a big decision to make,” he continued:
Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East, or even the world.
Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?
But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn’t make sense for them not to.
They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already and won in a landslide. We won in a giant landslide, and I’ll be here for two and a half years.
Previous Threats
The world has heard that eliminationist rhetoric at least twice before.
On April 7, Trump threatened to destroy the entire country and everything in it.
“A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” he said.
“I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”
Before that, on Easter Sunday, he threatened to starve the Iranian people to death and deprive them of electricity and water.
“Tuesday will be Power Plant Day, and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one, in Iran,” he wrote on Truth Social:
There will be nothing like it!!! Open the F****n’ Strait, you crazy b****rds, or you’ll be living in Hell – JUST WATCH! Praise be to Allah.
Former supporters unsparingly attacked Trump for the reckless threats.

sources.news_title: Trump says Iran deal near, Tehran offers Hormuz reopen
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has warned he could annihilate Iran if there's no deal to end the war, but also suggested an agreement could come soon, amid a diplomatic push at the United Nations.
"I have a big decision to make," Trump said in a speech at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? ... Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"
Iran's Armed Forces dismissed Trump's comments at the UN as "propaganda", saying their response is "full readiness to inflict more severe, crushing, and unpredictable blows on the aggressors".
But away from the fiery rhetoric, discussions continued to try to end the nearly seven-month conflict that began with joint US-Israeli strikes and has since killed thousands, driven up oil prices and drawn in neighbouring countries.
Trump said that envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran".
"I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal," he said.
Trump also met the leaders of Middle Eastern countries who are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of global oil and gas shipments before the war, but are wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
Many also host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war.
"We think that the situation with Iran could end right after the (November 3) midterm elections, maybe before. I don't know. You never know," Trump said as he met the leaders.
The diplomatic manoeuvring comes as Trump faces pressure on multiple fronts - rising energy costs at home, a widening regional conflict abroad, and the midterms six weeks away that could reshape his political standing.
A senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
The senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington through mediators last week and could reopen the strait to Gulf shipping within seven days if its demands were met.
In a reminder of Iran's firm position so far, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who headed Iran's negotiating team at previous talks, said Iran would never surrender: "Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces."
On the table is a Qatari proposal for a common security framework involving Iran and the Arab Gulf states, regional sources said. One source said Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war as Iran-aligned Houthi fighters have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight.
Oil markets did find some relief on Tuesday after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu within hours, albeit at reduced volumes.
The pipeline, Saudi Arabia's main export route bypassing wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, had been shut after attacks this month that Riyadh blamed on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq.
Australian Associated Press

Trump warns in U.N. speech he could ‘annihilate’ Iran without peace deal
UNITED NATIONS >> President Donald Trump used his U.N. General Assembly speech today to make the case for his war on Iran, arguing he has prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and warning that he could “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if no deal is reached to end the conflict.
While predicting his administration would strike a peace deal with Iran following the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, Trump called on other nations to join America in isolating Iran economically to force it to the negotiating table.
“I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
He later told reporters at the United Nations that U.S. officials had had a “very good” three-hour meeting today with the Iranian delegation.
Since returning to office last year for a second term, Trump has sent waves through the global order, joining Israel to attack Iran, ordering a raid on Venezuela that captured the country’s leader, and threatening to seize Greenland.
In a 37-minute speech ahead of a whirlwind diplomatic schedule that included meetings with the leaders of Britain, Ukraine and Japan, Trump laid out his foreign policy vision, arguing that the Iran war had spared the world the threat of a nuclear-armed menace while asserting U.S. dominance in the Western Hemisphere is essential to preventing crises from taking root.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” Trump said. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace.”
Outside the U.N. headquarters, dozens of anti-Iranian-government demonstrators gathered, a few of them holding up signs calling for democracy and decrying dictatorship.
Trump brushed aside suggestions that the midterm elections, in which his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress, could constrain his handling of the war. Some analysts have argued that a Democratic takeover of the legislature would weaken his leverage in the conflict.
“What they don’t realize is that I’m not running,” Trump said, referring to the leadership in Tehran. “I did that already, and won in a landslide. We won in a giant landslide, and I’ll be here for 2-1/2 years.”
Taking aim at U.S. neighbors, Trump labeled Mexico “the epicenter of cartel violence,” urged its government to “reclaim control of its soil,” and said his administration was pursuing “a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba.”
Members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump referenced his pressure campaign against the country.
“It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” said Trump.
Yet Trump’s appearance was less dramatic than in 2025, when he used a combative speech to chastise world leaders, warning that some countries were “going to hell,” and complained about U.N. facilities after being briefly stranded on a malfunctioning escalator and suffering an initial teleprompter failure.
Trump renewed his criticism of the U.N., highlighting his efforts to cut its bureaucracy, but offered no fresh attacks or indications that the U.S. would leave any additional U.N. agencies.
Trump spoke less than a week after a U.N. fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces committed war crimes in two strikes on Iran, including one that hit a primary school in the southern city of Minab.
He renewed his criticism of international bodies that could serve as a check on U.S. power, singling out the International Criminal Court and declaring that U.S. military personnel would not be subject to its authority.
“We will never allow U.S. service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said.
Ahead of a U.N. Security Council meeting on AI and international security on Wednesday, Trump acknowledged the challenges of the new technology but said, “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
The speech kicked off a day of high-level diplomacy at the United Nations, where Trump was due to meet more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine continued to test his foreign policy agenda.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had “established a good connection” with Trump in their first-ever meeting, where they discussed trade, Ukraine and the status of the Falkland Islands.
At the press-facing start of their talks, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the meeting would demonstrate the strength of the U.S.-Japan alliance amid a “severe security environment, including in Asia,” an apparent nod to China. Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later this week.
On his meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, Trump told reporters that the two talked about finding a solution to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Trump threatens to "annihilate" Iran and its people in UN address
sources.text:
President Trump’s rambling, combative speech Tuesday to the United Nations General Assembly saw him return to his most serious quagmire yet—the war in Iran—telling world leaders that he was considering completely destroying the country as a means to end the conflict he launched alongside Israel in February.
“Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” Trump pondered aloud, claiming that Iran’s leadership had rejected multiple peace deals with the US.

The Center for International Policy’s Matt Duss, a former Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) foreign policy adviser, said in a statement that Trump’s threats were “dangerously unhinged” and “must be unequivocally rejected.”
“Such rhetoric is not merely reckless, it is a criminal threat of genocide against an entire nation,” Duss wrote. “U.S. lawmakers and U.S. partners around the world should condemn Trump’s remarks.”
The president again framed his demand as centering on Iran’s nuclear program, despite offering up a shifting litany of goals and terms on which he’d end the war across the last seven months, and implied that scorched earth was the only alternative. Trump returned to the UN General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Tehran.
Nevertheless, Trump argued in his speech that the world was better off under his auspices.
"As president of the most extraordinary nation in history," Trump said. "I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester."

(OSV News) — President Donald Trump said Sept. 22 during a speech to the United Nations General Assembly that he has a decision to make on Iran: to make a deal or to “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”
Trump’s comments — repeating a threat Pope Leo, Catholic bishops and other world leaders denounced as morally unjustifiable — came as he reached his lowest-ever approval rating on foreign affairs in a CNN/SSRS survey. Just 29% of U.S. adults said they approve of his performance on foreign affairs, with pollsters attributing the downturn to the Iran war.
“But I have a big decision to make: Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump said during the speech. “Maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East, or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Trump speculates Iran deal to come after midterms
Trump said he believes “we’ll make a deal right after the election.”
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running,” he said. “I did that already and won in a landslide. I gave absolutely no credence, and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump’s remarks that he is not on the ballot come just a few weeks after he urged his fellow Republicans at their midterm convention to “pretend” he is on the November ballot.
After the U.S. and Israel initiated war with Iran in February, arguing as they did so that the Iranian regime presented grave nuclear threats, Iran effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping route, by striking ships there. The closure of the strait has led to a significant global spike in energy costs, which is among the factors driving opposition to the conflict among most U.S. adults, polls show.
Comments echo earlier threats condemned by Church
Trump said during his speech he first sought a diplomatic resolution to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon but claimed “they absolutely refused.”
“That was a big mistake,” he said.
Trump previously threatened in April to wipe out Iran’s “whole civilization,” but later backed down, citing negotiations with Pakistani mediators. Catholic leaders, including Pope Leo XIV, were among those who condemned the threat at the time. Archbishop Paul S. Coakley of Oklahoma City, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, echoed Pope Leo, emphasizing, “The threat of destroying a whole civilization and the intentional targeting of civilian infrastructure cannot be morally justified.”
Pope Leo has objected to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran as unjust, and called for a return to diplomacy. Trump lashed out repeatedly at Pope Leo in response, claiming he supported Iran having nuclear weapons; however, the pope never made any such statement. Pope Leo has consistently called for the rejection of nuclear weapons, and for peace and dialogue in the region.

“Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon. Superintelligence,” he said as he urged other countries to follow suit.
Multiple tech leaders have recently called for a slowdown in AI development to establish safety guardrails, prompting debate on Capitol Hill about how to respond.
The U.S. Catholic bishops’ administrative committee also met with tech leaders earlier in September and formed a task force to safeguard human dignity as AI rapidly evolves in line with Pope Leo XVI’s encyclical on AI, “Magnifica Humanitas.” The pope called for “adequate regulatory tools capable of upholding justice and curbing the distorting effects of technological power,” and a dozen U.S. bishops met with members of Congress on Sept. 16 to urge lawmakers to enact effective safety guardrails on AI.

Trump, however, has largely rejected these concerns around AI, taking a bullish position on the advancement of the technology, a position he reiterated in his UN speech.
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.
Also during his time in New York for the U.N. General Assembly, Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement Sept. 22 permitting a larger US military presence on Greenland.
Trump had previously stated the U.S. would seek to acquire Greenland, even by use of force, before later backing down.

Trump then raised the alternative of using American military power to “annihilate the Islamic Republic,” warning that Washington would not allow the Iranian government to continue threatening other nations. His remarks represented one of his most direct warnings to Tehran since the United States began its military campaign earlier this year.
Despite the forceful language, Trump maintained that a diplomatic settlement remains possible. He predicted that Iran may agree to a deal after the November 3 midterm elections, although he insisted that domestic political considerations are not influencing his decisions.

Trump also called on other governments to increase economic pressure on Tehran and help force its leaders back to the negotiating table. His administration has imposed sweeping sanctions designed to isolate Iran from the global financial system and prevent the government from rebuilding its military capabilities.
The president’s position leaves Tehran with an increasingly narrow set of options. Iran has signaled that it is open to negotiations, but its leaders have demanded an easing of American military and economic pressure. The two governments remain divided over Iran’s nuclear program, its ballistic missile arsenal and control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has repeatedly said that Iran will never be permitted to obtain a nuclear weapon. The White House has identified dismantling Tehran’s missile production, destroying its naval capabilities and cutting off support for regional terrorist groups as central objectives of the campaign.

The narrow waterway connects major Persian Gulf oil producers to global markets and carries a significant share of the world’s petroleum supply. Disruptions in the region have driven energy prices higher and increased pressure on governments seeking to prevent the conflict from spreading.
Trump urged Iran to fully reopen the strait while describing American naval operations intended to protect commercial shipping. He argued that a lasting agreement could quickly ease pressure on oil markets and allow Iran to begin restoring its economy.
Oil prices reacted to the president’s remarks as traders weighed the possibility that negotiations could be delayed until after the midterm elections. He also claimed that direct communication between Washington and Tehran was continuing and that Iranian officials still wanted an agreement.
Trump did not announce a deadline for Iran to accept a deal. His address nevertheless made clear that he views the current pause as temporary and expects Tehran to make substantial concessions.
The president’s message combined an offer of economic recovery with an unmistakable military threat: Iran can negotiate from its weakened position or face a renewed American campaign intended to permanently eliminate its ability to wage war.

sources.news_title: Defending the Iran war, Trump tells UN he must decide whether to 'annihilate' Islamic Republic
sources.text:
UNITED NATIONS | President Donald Trump returned to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday at a tumultuous moment for the world — and for his presidency — and made the case that he’s shown fortitude while other leaders have equivocated as he defended his decision to start a war with Iran.
But Trump also suggested that he could be at a crossroads in the conflict even as he called on the Islamic Republic to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to the negotiating table to find a settlement to end the conflict.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
The president’s comments came in his wide-ranging address to the international body in which he also celebrated this year’s U.S. military operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from power, a new agreement to expand the U.S. military presence in Greenland, and pushed back against calls for greater regulation of the artificial intelligence industry.
But at the heart of the address was a fulsome defense of the war and pushback on the notion that Iran has shown a measure of resilience.
“The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate,” Trump said.
Trump also accused Iran of stalling to make a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and negotiate an endgame to the war until after the midterm elections in the United States. He insisted the tactic would have no effect on how he approaches the conflict.
Most of Iran’s delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump railed against the Islamic Republic.
Trump’s speech began a busy day of diplomacy
After his speech, Trump gathered with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the General Assembly to sign a new security agreement.
The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to “take over” Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary. Trump said Tuesday the U.S. will immediately begin the process of developing a larger military presence in Greenland including “building two very major military bases.”
Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark’s territory.
Trump also held talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The leaders said they discussed migration, the conflict in Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war and more.
Trump also met with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Later, he’ll meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and will hold a more informal meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez, according to the White House.
He’s also scheduled to meet with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates — to discuss the way ahead with the war in Iran and growing concern about recent Iran-backed rebel attacks on Saudi Arabia. Trump also plans to take part in an event on the Shield of Americas, an initiative Trump launched with Latin American countries earlier this year focused on combatting violent cartels.
Iran war looms large at General Assembly
The visit to the U.N. comes when Trump’s foreign policy approach — particularly his decision to start a war with Iran — has become a drag on his fellow Republicans’ hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections. Nevertheless, Trump made the case in his speech that the world is better off for his leadership.
“As president of the most extraordinary nation in history,” Trump said. “I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester.”
In last year’s address at the U.N., Trump claimed the U.S. had “demolished” Iran’s nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities.
He returned to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran.
The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran’s top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles.
The energy market continues to be spooked by the war and oil prices remain elevated. Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane.
But Trump insisted anew that the elevated oil prices are a transitory problem that will fade once the war ends.
“Oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict,” Trump said. “And they were very low in the United States. They were really low.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Trump is open to meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, while he’s in New York for the General Assembly.
“This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you’re going to solve problems,” Rubio said on NBC’s “Today” show. “It doesn’t mean you’re going to end up agreeing with them, but it’s important.”
Trump’s frustration with Russia-Ukraine war mounts
The president also touched on Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine during his U.N. address — a conflict that during his 2024 campaign he predicted would be resolved on Day One of his second term. He once again expressed hope that the conflict will soon be resolved.
Trump hasn’t obscured that his patience is being tested by Ukraine’s targeting of Russia’s diesel refineries — an issue that’s added to the global oil markets’ volatility — and Russia’s targeting of Ukraine’s energy grid.
Trump last week asserted that he got the two sides to agree to not target each other’s energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy, who is scheduled to meet with Trump on Tuesday afternoon, said he was willing to go along with Trump’s plan if Russia abided by it. Russia said it could only go along with Trump’s energy truce proposal if Western energy sanctions on Moscow were lifted first.
The two sides have continued carrying out strikes on refineries and other energy infrastructure.
Trump noted that last week he signed a new sanctions bill targeting Moscow. It empowers him to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas.
The legislation includes an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Trump, however, has yet to enact the stiff penalties.
“If necessary, I will have to use them,” Trump said. “It’s time to stop the killing.”
Associated Press Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee contributed to this story.

Trump talks tough on Iran, even as he predicts diplomatic deal after midterms
Addressing the UNGA, Trump wondered, ‘Will a deal be made … or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic?’
Brendan Smialowski-Pool/Getty Images
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he faces a “big decision” between making a deal with Iran and escalating military conflict, as he predicted the sides would reach an agreement following the midterm elections.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump told the U.N. General Assembly in New York, on the first day of the high-level week. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? … Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
The president has recently made similar statements suggesting he must choose between negotiations and further confrontation, though there appear to be no serious negotiations underway and U.S. strikes have been sporadic.
"I have a big decision to make,” Trump said at the UN. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? … Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic? … I believe we’ll make a deal right after the [midterm] election.” pic.twitter.com/LYB5f2i0Fd
— Jewish Insider (@jewishinsider) September 22, 2026
Trump said he believes an agreement with Iran will ultimately be reached after the U.S. midterm elections in November, arguing that Tehran is waiting to see how Republicans perform.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the [midterm] election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realize is that I’m not running.”
Even absent a deal, Trump argued that U.S. efforts in Iran have yielded success, including stopping Iran from being the “bully” of the Middle East.
“For 51 years, the fanatical Iranian regime has ruled by bloodshed and mass murder, spreading death and carnage and chaos across the entire Middle East and beyond,” Trump said. “They were the bully of the Middle East, but they are the bully no more.”
While no bilateral sit-downs between Trump and Iranian leadership were scheduled, Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that White House Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had a “very good meeting” with Iranian officials on Tuesday.
“It was a meeting that lasted for three hours … They had a very good meeting, very productive meeting, and they have another one scheduled in the near future,” Trump said. “We’ll see how it turns out, but, certainly, it’s to their advantage to make a deal, and if we can do that, it’s preferable.”
Prior to the meeting a U.S. official had told CNN that Trump said he would be open to arranging a meeting with Iranian officials in New York “if the conditions are right,” or delegating senior advisors traveling with him to meet with them. Axios further reported that mediating Arab countries had been trying to arrange a meeting as well.
Trump called on “all nations” to “join us in enforcing the complete economic isolation of Iran until they stop their attacks on commercial shipping, relinquish their nuclear ambitions and cease their support of terror.”
Praising international support for Washington’s stance, Trump thanked the U.N. Security Council for passing a resolution in March condemning Iranian attacks on maritime trade.
“That resolution, I’m pleased to say, received more co-sponsors from U.N. member nations than any Security Council resolution in history,” Trump said. “That’s something. Now we must be equally united in maintaining pressure.”
He added that the U.S. Navy has recently escorted more than 1 billion barrels of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz, maintaining that “more oil is flowing than at any point since the start of the war.”
He also dismissed reports suggesting the U.S. military is running dangerously low on munitions as a result of the conflict.
“We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before. We are adding to our stockpiles faster than we have ever been able to do before,” he said.
Trump noted that 18 new munitions facilities are currently under construction by defense contractors, promising that the expansion will lead to the “very rapid deployment of missiles of every type and ammunition of every type,” as well as faster resupply for allies.
Turning to the Middle East more broadly, Trump touched on the situation in Gaza, where implementation of his administration’s 20-point peace plan remains stalled as Hamas refuses to disarm. The president thanked countries that joined the Board of Peace, as well as those that committed personnel to secure Gaza.
“We ended the war in Gaza, saving untold thousands of lives. We also brought home all the remaining hostages, both living and dead, every single one of them,” Trump said. “Nearly 30 countries have joined the board, which I am honored to chair, and we’re thankful to many of those member nations for contributing billions and billions of dollars to relief. I also want to thank those who have committed troops, police, and training to help stabilize Gaza, including Indonesia, Morocco, Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan, Egypt, Jordan and more.”

sources.news_title: Trump Threatens Iran With Further Military Action, Predicts Post-Midterm Deal in U.N. Speech
sources.text:
President Donald Trump used his U.N. General Assembly address to warn Iran of further military action while predicting an eventual agreement, calling for tighter economic isolation of Tehran and defending U.S. operations from Venezuela to the Strait of Hormuz.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
President Donald Trump delivered a sweeping defense of American military and economic power before the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, threatening substantially greater action against Iran if diplomacy fails while predicting that Tehran ultimately will reach an agreement with Washington after the November midterm elections.
WATCH:
The president devoted a significant portion of his 37-minute address to the nearly seven-month conflict with Iran, portraying Tehran as facing a choice between negotiations that would allow it to rebuild or another round of potentially devastating U.S. attacks.
“Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?” Trump asked.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Despite the warning, Trump said he expects the confrontation to end through an agreement rather than another major escalation.
“But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.
“What they don’t realize is that I’m not running.”
Trump said Iranian leaders may believe the results of the Nov. 3 congressional elections could change Washington’s position, but he argued his approach would remain focused on preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon regardless of the domestic political outcome. Reuters reported that Trump simultaneously called for Iran’s economic isolation while predicting a post-election agreement.
“From the first day I entered the political arena, I’ve been unwavering. I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump portrayed the current confrontation as the result of Tehran rejecting repeated diplomatic opportunities while continuing to develop missiles, drones and other military capabilities capable of threatening U.S. forces and regional countries.
He pointed to Operation Midnight Hammer, the 2025 U.S. strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities, saying it had “obliterated their nuclear program beneath mountains of rubble.”
He also defended Operation Epic Fury, the U.S.-Israeli military campaign launched against Iran in February, and described Iranian military losses in sweeping terms.
“As a result of Operation Epic Fury, all 159 ships of their Navy are now lying at the bottom of the sea,” Trump said.
“Likewise, their air force is gone. Their radar is gone, their anti-aircraft equipment is gone. Their missiles and drone manufacturing capacity is almost gone.”
Those figures represented Trump’s characterization of the military campaign. The White House has previously said Operation Epic Fury was intended to destroy Iran’s missile-production capacity, cripple its naval forces and prevent it from acquiring a nuclear weapon, while public U.S. military reporting during the operation documented substantial but evolving Iranian naval losses.
Trump also accused Iran of violating a ceasefire and attacking civilian commercial shipping, tying the military confrontation to continued disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz.
“I call on all nations to join us in enforcing the complete economic isolation of Iran until they stop their attacks on commercial shipping, relinquish their nuclear ambitions, and cease their support of terror,” he said.
The United States has already imposed an extensive economic blockade on Iran, while American forces have been escorting commercial vessels through the strategically critical waterway.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, said Saturday that American forces had supported the transit of more than 1 billion barrels of crude oil and more than 2,000 commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in recent months.
Trump cited those operations Tuesday as evidence that U.S. military power was keeping international energy supplies moving despite the conflict.
The president also pushed back against concerns that months of operations in the Middle East have strained American ammunition inventories.
“We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before,” Trump said.
Trump said 18 new munitions plants were being constructed.
His claim came amid conflicting assessments over U.S. stockpiles. CBS News reported that the Pentagon inspector general recently identified “strategic inventory shortfalls” resulting from the Iran conflict, even as Trump rejected suggestions that American forces faced meaningful shortages.
The president placed the Iran confrontation within a broader argument that his administration’s willingness to combine military force, tariffs, trade pressure and personal diplomacy had resolved conflicts that conventional diplomacy had failed to settle.
Trump said he had helped settle eight wars, a claim his administration has repeatedly promoted as part of what it describes as a “peace through strength” foreign policy.
He also pointed to the Gaza agreement.
“We also brought home all remaining hostages, both living and dead. Every single one of them,” Trump said.
The United Nations’ Board of Peace reported earlier this year that all hostages had been returned under the Gaza framework, while humanitarian assistance had expanded and a ceasefire had largely held. The board said 28 countries had joined the organization by that stage.
Trump thanked the U.N. Security Council for endorsing his 20-point Gaza peace plan and said nearly 30 countries had become part of the Board of Peace, which he chairs.
The president presented Gaza as an example of cooperation between Washington, regional governments and international institutions that he said produced results after years of conflict.
Ukraine remains one of the major wars Trump has not resolved.
He nevertheless expressed confidence that negotiations involving Moscow and Kyiv would eventually produce an agreement.
“We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done,” Trump said.
Reuters reported that Trump added that he believed progress could come “more quickly than people understand,” though he announced no ceasefire or settlement Tuesday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was among the world leaders Trump was scheduled to meet after the speech as the administration continued discussing air defenses, sanctions and possible measures to reduce attacks on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping.
Trump also devoted part of the address to Venezuela, where a U.S. military operation earlier this year captured Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face federal charges.
Washington subsequently entered into a major energy agreement with Venezuela’s interim government involving development rights and U.S. majority control associated with an estimated 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves.
“To the victor belong the spoils,” Trump said.
He framed the Venezuela operation not only as a change in U.S. policy toward Caracas but as a demonstration of how Washington intends to approach security threats throughout the Western Hemisphere.
“And if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump said.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” Trump said elsewhere in the address. Reuters reported that he used the operation to argue that American military dominance was necessary to deter threats throughout the region.
His remarks also came as the administration expanded pressure on drug cartels, Cuba and other governments and organizations in the Americas.
Trump described Mexico as an “epicenter of cartel violence” and called on its government to strengthen control over territory affected by criminal organizations. He also said his administration was pursuing a fundamental change in Cuba, prompting members of the Cuban delegation to leave the General Assembly hall during his remarks.
The speech repeatedly returned to Trump’s broader argument that American strength — rather than restraint or reliance primarily on international institutions — had produced diplomatic leverage.
“While others have talked, I have acted,” Trump said, according to CBS News. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them. While others have talked of courage, America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world.”
Trump also criticized international institutions that he believes constrain American sovereignty, including the International Criminal Court.
He said the United States would not accept ICC jurisdiction over American military personnel and encouraged countries belonging to the court to reconsider their participation.
“We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” Trump said.
The president nevertheless stopped short of rejecting the United Nations itself.
He argued that the organization could serve a useful function if it moved away from policies he considers ideological and focused more heavily on conflict resolution and international security.
Iran remained the dominant immediate question.
Trump’s address came the same day a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran also indicated that its delegation in New York had authority to pursue diplomatic contacts through intermediaries.
Trump’s public remarks offered no acceptance of those specific conditions.
Instead, he called for increased international economic pressure and warned that the alternative to a settlement could be another major military campaign.
Hours later, however, Trump said the United States and Iran were continuing to communicate and that he believed a settlement ultimately would be reached.
That left the administration advancing pressure and diplomacy simultaneously: urging other governments to isolate Tehran while publicly forecasting an eventual agreement.
Trump’s message to the General Assembly was that the decision now rests with Iran.
His administration, he said, remains committed to preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and is prepared to use economic and military power to enforce that objective, while leaving open a diplomatic route that could allow Iran to rebuild under a negotiated settlement.

sources.text:
Trump weighs 'big decision' on Iran, rejects AI push in major UN speech on 'American power'
In short:
Donald Trump has said he must decide whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic" during a speech to world leaders at the UN.
A day after many countries asked the UN to consider creating a supervisory body for AI, Mr Trump said the US would reject efforts to "construct a globalist scheme" to control the technology.
What's next?
More than 100 world leaders, including Anthony Albanese, will address the UN General Assembly as part of its annual high-level week.
US President Donald Trump has used a speech at the UN to portray "American power" as the solution to the world's problems, defending his ongoing war with Iran and declaring he now must decide whether to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic.
Mr Trump also said the US would reject any international scheme to put controls on artificial intelligence.
The comment came just a day after 22 world leaders, including Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, signed a statement calling for global guardrails.
Mr Trump's address, delivered six weeks before the US's midterm elections, amounted to a pushback against growing criticism that his administration's actions abroad were harming the US and creating a more destabilised and dangerous world.
"We're reasserting American power, including American military power, where necessary, in our region and around the world to create a safer future for all of us," Mr Trump said.
"While others have talked, I have acted," he said.
"While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace."
With the war with Iran approaching the seven-month mark and no end in sight, Mr Trump said he was facing a "big decision": Strike a deal that allowed Iran to rebuild or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".
"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations?" he said, as a representative for Iran's delegation sat stony-faced in the audience.
"But I believe we'll make a deal right after the election because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election."
Mr Trump later said US and Iranian officials held a "very good meeting" over several hours on the sidelines of the summit.
Previous peace talks between the two countries have failed to make meaningful progress since a preliminary agreement was signed by both nations in June.
During his speech, Mr Trump suggested Cuba was the US's next target, predicting its communist dictatorship "will fall", but also saying "let's see what happens" in negotiations with the US.
His comments prompted a walk-out by the Cuban delegation.
He also used his address to predict, as he has repeatedly in the past, that he would end the Russia-Ukraine war soon.
"It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand," he said.
Renaming AI and rejecting regulation
On the dangers of AI, which Mr Trump has been downplaying as a "hoax", he conceded there was a need to "be careful".
But he also said the US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now".
The comment represented a smackdown of a global body proposed by a coalition of middle power nations, including Australia, in a statement signed on the sidelines of the summit yesterday.
In a surprise announcement, Mr Trump also said he was "changing the name" of AI.
He said he was ordering the US government to start referring to "artificial intelligence" as "super intelligence" in all official documents, and he hoped the world would follow.
"The use of the word 'artificial' makes intelligence fake. It makes it sound fake and it is not fake,"
"It's actually amazing."
The term "superintelligence" is already defined as an advanced form of artificial intelligence that exceeds human capabilities.
Some experts have warned superintelligence represents one of the greatest risks AI could pose to humanity, and US politicians including independent senator Bernie Sanders have proposed a ban on its development.
Mr Trump was one of the first heads of state to address the UN General Assembly high-level week, the UN's annual gathering of world leaders in New York.
He was expected to hold a series of sideline meetings after his speech, including with Gulf state leaders whose countries have borne the brunt of Iran's retaliatory missile and drone strikes.
Mr Albanese will address the body later this week.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump at U.N.: Stopping Iran Regime 'a Reality We Had to Confront'
sources.text:
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said ending the Iran regime’s ability to sponsor terror around the world and its quest to obtain nuclear weapons was “a reality we had to confront” upon entering his second term in office.
Trump opened his speech discussing his domestic accomplishments, highlighted by adding one million new jobs, reducing violent crime levels, and beautifying Washington, DC, the nation’s capital.
He said he inherited a dark age from the previous administration and since entered a “golden age” of a newly energized and powerful United States.
Pivoting to Iran, Trump said he “acted with decisiveness and speed to reshape the world stage and solve problems that have plagued us for far too long. I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester; they only become harder to solve. So while others have talked, I have acted. While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them.”
Continuing, Trump said America has shown courage while others have only talked about it, and worked with many of the nations represented at the U.N. to solve challenges and settle years of unfinished business.
Calling Iran’s regime a danger that gathered strength, he called out the number one sponsor of terror and said their fanatical regime rules by bloodshed and mass murder and spreads death, carnage, and chaos across the Middle East and beyond. “They are the bully no more,” said Trump.
He traced the current conflict back to when he entered the political arena, saying he held an unwavering belief and would never allow Iran to develop nuclear weapons. Trump campaigned in 2016 on ending the Obama-led Iran deal that gave the regime billions of dollars.
Trump said that after entering office in January 2025, he offered Iran full economic cooperation in exchange for permanently ending their nuclear weapons program and support for terror organizations. He said the regime refused, and that it was a big mistake for them do so.
In 2025’s Operation Midnight Hammer, Trump said he “obliterated” their nuclear program beneath mountains of rubble and urged them at that point to make a deal, which the regime again refused. He said they continued to build missile drone stockpiles that threatened the security of American servicemembers and other countries in the region, noting some of their missiles were capable of reaching Europe, something Trump said he hopes the Europeans realize.
“Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional ballistic missile shield,” Trump stated. “If they had succeeded, that wicked regime would have been free to spread terror and death forever, knowing that any attempt to stop them would face an arsenal of nuclear annihilation.”
Trump noted that the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terror attack that killed nearly 3,000 Americans was just 11 days ago and a few miles from the U.N., and that in just two weeks would be the third anniversary of the terror attack that killed 1,200 Israeli civilians, the worst attack in that country’s history.
The October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas terrorists against Israel was funded by Iran’s regime and killed 46 Americans and took a dozen more hostage. Trump noted that October 7 terrorists tortured and mutilated children and babies, something Iran’s Supreme Leader celebrated and called “a service to humanity.”
Trump added that Iran’s regime has slaughtered tens of thousands of its own citizens this year for protesting and asked those in the chamber to imagine a regime allowed to carry out large-scale terror attacks behind a nuclear shield.
“This was the reality we had to confront,” Trump said, adding it was something too many preferred to ignore, including past presidents and other leaders. “They were unwilling to do anything about it but they knew the problem. After giving Iran every chance for a deal, I took action to ensure that neither the United States or any nation would have to face such a nightmare.”
This was the basis for Operation Epic Fury, Trump said. The president rattled off the statistics of the operations, saying their entire Naval fleet was at the bottom of the sea, their air force was gone, and their anti-aircraft missiles were gone. Trump added the only thing that isn’t gone is inflation, which has reached over 300 percent.
Trump continued, saying that after agreeing to a ceasefire the regime once again launched brazen acts of terror against ships. He thanked the U.N. Security Council for passing resolutions condemning the attacks against commercial shipping.
He said maintaining pressure against the regime is essential and that the United States Navy has escorted more than one billion barrels of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz.
In concluding his Iran comments Trump said he had a big decision: making a deal letting them rebuild or annihilating the Islamic republic and never giving them a chance to kill and destroy again. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness?”
The president said he believes he can make a deal following the November midterm election. He said the regime didn’t realize he was not running.
“I’ll be here for 2 and a half years… I give no credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” to a round of applause interrupting the speech and ending his comments on the Iran conflict.

sources.news_title: Trump threatens to annihilate Iran or deal after midterms at UN
sources.text:
President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that he faces a "big decision" on whether to "annihilate" Iran or negotiate a deal to end the war — and predicted the outcome would come after the November midterm elections.
The president gave the address as the war with Iran approaches its eighth month with no clear end in sight
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?" Trump said during his roughly 37-minute address. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"
Trump said he believes a deal will come "right after the election," adding that Iran is "waiting to see how I do in the midterm election." He dismissed the notion that the vote would influence his decision. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running," he said. "The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
Trump defended his decision to launch the war, framing it as a necessary response to Iran's pursuit of a nuclear weapon. He also dismissed reports of diminished U.S. munitions stockpiles, saying "we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using." The Pentagon's own inspector general has found that the war has led to "strategic inventory shortfalls" of munitions, according to CBS News.
The speech came one week after the UN's Human Rights Council released a report concluding there were "reasonable grounds to believe" that U.S. forces had committed war crimes in February strikes on an Iranian school and a residential neighborhood, according to NBC News.
Beyond Iran, Trump touted a military agreement with Greenland and Denmark, signed later Tuesday, that he said gives the U.S. control over security in the Arctic territory. He also pointed to U.S. intervention in Venezuela as evidence that Washington would not permit threats to the Western Hemisphere. The Cuban delegation walked out of the hall after Trump said his administration is seeking a "fundamental change" in Cuba and that the country "will fall."
On artificial intelligence, Trump announced a push to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "superintelligence" in government documents, contending that the word "artificial" unfairly undermines the technology by making it "sound fake." He vowed that Washington would "encourage" the technology's growth and drew a parallel between people raising alarms about AI and those who have long warned about climate change.
Trump is scheduled to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and leaders of Gulf Cooperation Council states later Tuesday, with Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to the White House set for Thursday.
