sources.news_title: ‘Into hell’: Trump signals aggressive lame-duck foreign policy at UN
sources.text:
‘Into hell’: Trump signals aggressive lame-duck foreign policy at UN
President tells General Assembly he could ‘annihilate the Islamic Republic’ of Iran
ANALYSIS — President Donald Trump’s unapologetic and chest-thumping address Tuesday before the U.N. General Assembly signaled an aggressive lame-duck foreign policy that will continue to reframe the world order.
He stepped to the lectern in the massive hall in New York City for the fifth time — his 2020 General Assembly address was delivered virtually, during the COVID-19 pandemic — now at war with the White House press corps, Iran and several Tehran-backed proxy groups. Trump let the world know he had no intention to change course at home or abroad.
“We have acted with decisiveness and speed to reshape the world stage and solve problems that have plagued us for far too long,” he told other world leaders. “As president of the most extraordinary nation in history, I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester — they only become harder to solve.”
His second-term foreign policy has so far been detached from his “America first” 2024 campaign slogan. Nothing reflects his defiant global approach this term more than his standoff with Iran. The native New Yorker conjured his inner Tony Soprano as he essentially said “fuggetaboutit” to critics who want him to cut a deal with Iran’s remaining leaders and end a conflict that has driven up global gasoline and energy prices.
“I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he said, warning that Iran was pursuing “an arsenal of nuclear annihilation,” which he once claimed U.S. bomber strikes last year had “obliterated,” before recently dropping that claim.
“But I have a big decision to make: Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic — and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?” Trump said, his tone turning more serious.
He said he could choose to use military strikes to “drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations,” before adding that he still believes “we’ll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn’t make sense for them not to.”
His intransigence towards Iran, some Republicans worry, could be a major thorn in the side of their party’s congressional candidates in November’s midterm elections. A RealClearPolitics average of several recent polls gives Democrats an 8.3 percentage point advantage on a generic congressional ballot.
Trump’s disapproval level on his handling of the Iran conflict hit 60 percent in a YouGov-The Economist survey conducted Sept. 11-14, with 33 percent voicing approval. Sixty-six percent of respondents disapproved of Trump’s handling of inflation, with 29 percent approving, according to the same poll.
Trump did not spell out a path to an end to the conflict with Iran, which energy analysts say likely will help trigger a further spike in gas prices in the United States in the midterms’ final stretch.
Trump appeared unconcerned with his lack of an exit plan or about how the nearly seven-month-old conflict could affect his party’s attempt to retain control of the House and Senate. If Democrats win the House, they would have investigative and subpoena powers to pull back the layers of the onion that has been his second term. In fact, the day after Election Day appeared to be his lone path out of the stalemate.
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said of Iran. “What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I’ll be here for two-and-a-half years.”
“The Republican Party is running, and I’ll be helping them,” he said.
He then delivered hawkish claims about his administration working with U.S. defense firms to fast-track new missiles and ammunition. And he called on U.N. member countries to “join us in enforcing the complete economic isolation of Iran until they stop their attacks on commercial shipping, relinquish their nuclear ambitions and cease their support of terror.”
Russia and Ukraine
He also did not detail any new plan to try ending the bloody Russia-Ukraine war, which candidate Trump in 2024 promised to end on the first day of his second term. More than 600 days since he returned to power, the fighting in Eastern Europe rages, with recent Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy targets also, analysts say, risking another gas price hike.
All he offered Tuesday was a version of the same years-old but unfulfilled line: “We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done. It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand,” he said.
In many ways, Trump’s latest General Assembly address offers a juxtaposition to his acceptance speech on election night in November 2016, showing how much his foreign policy philosophy has evolved. Back then, he described himself as a once-in-a-generation figure who would heal all of America’s ailments at home — largely by diminishing its role as a global leader and ending its post-9/11 military conflicts.
“So while others have talked, I have acted. While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them,” he said. “While others have talked of courage, America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world.”
‘Will not allow’
To a silent hall, he boasted about the U.S. military action in Venezuela that nabbed Nicolás Maduro and led to a still-vague oil deal between the two countries. He again resisted robust artificial-intelligence regulation by casting AI as an economic growth engine for the U.S. And notably, he sounded skeptical about ongoing diplomatic talks with Cuba’s government, which are being led by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba” because “it’s an absolutely failed state,” Trump said. “We will not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep, right at our doorstep.”
The speech showed again how Trump 2.0 — even more than the first Trump presidency — has reshaped Washington’s standing around the world, its growing distance from traditional allies and his own willingness to embrace hardliners.
But Michael McFaul, U.S. ambassador to Russia under President Barack Obama from 2012 to 2014, wrote recently on Substack that while “Trumpism” at home likely will last for some time after he leaves office, foreign policy could be a different story.
“Without question, President Trump has done real damage to American power and purpose in global affairs in ways that will take years, if not decades, to repair. His second term has wreaked more havoc than his first,” wrote McFaul, now a professor at Stanford University. “But to assume that this current trajectory is permanent is analytically inaccurate and prescriptively dangerous.”
“In his second term, Trump has not followed or reflected the will of the majority on foreign policy. Instead, he has pursued a series of foreign policy initiatives driven solely by his own desires,” McFaul added. “Trump the individual, not innate structural forces, is the cause of much of the irrational, imprudent chaos unfolding in American foreign policy today. … Change is possible. Change is even probable.”
But that kind of sweeping foreign policy change, regardless of November’s winners, is still two elections and 18 months away.
“Last week, in honor of Sen. Lindsey Graham, I signed a powerful new law passed by Congress, providing me with enormous new tariff authorities,” Trump said. “And if necessary, I will have to use them.”
Murmuring among the assembled leaders began even before he had left the room, after reminding them he would not be leaving the world stage anytime soon.

sources.news_title: Trump Tells UN: ‘Big Decision’ Coming on Iran, Threatens To ‘Annihilate the Islamic Republic’ and Drive Regime ‘Into Hell With No Chance of Survival’
sources.text:
TURTLE BAY—President Donald Trump told global leaders on Tuesday afternoon that he is facing "a big decision" on the war with Iran and will "drive them into hell with no chance of survival" if Tehran refuses to compromise at the bargaining table.
"I have a big decision to make," Trump said on the opening day of the United Nations General Assembly. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?"
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump continued. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"
Trump made clear his decision will rest solely on Tehran's willingness to relinquish its nuclear program, end support for terror groups, and curtail its ballistic missile program. The president suggested that Iran may be stalling peace talks until after America's midterm elections, but he made clear that the politics of the day will not influence his final decision.
"What they don't realize is that I'm not running," he said. "I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind." The United States and Iran, he added, "will definitely get it done. We will get it done one way or the other. It's going to be done. It's going to be done fast."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking Tuesday morning on NBC's Today show, left open the possibility that Trump would meet with Iran's president on the sidelines of this week's gathering.
"I don't think anything is scheduled at this point, but we're certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about, and that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon," Rubio said.
Trump's keynote U.N. address, a White House official told the Washington Free Beacon, was meant to remind the world that he "is using American Power to confront longstanding challenges and reshape the world to America's benefit." From Iran to Gaza and other areas of conflict, "President Trump has acted" to ensure a "safer and more prosperous world for the American People—and a much more powerful America," the official said.
A large portion of Trump's speech focused on the United Nations itself and its capitulation to "the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected."
"There is no global government, and while I'm president, there will be no global taxes," Trump said, referring to an aborted bid by the U.N. International Maritime Organization to impose a global carbon tax that would have raised international shipping costs by an estimated 10 to 20 percent.
The president also reserved harsh words for the International Criminal Court, an "out of control institution" run by "an evil group of people." Trump said the court's efforts to prosecute American military members and Israeli officials for supposed war crimes will never happen on his watch. He implored all U.N. member nations to "officially resign from this rogue institution."
The White House official said that Trump's criticism of the United Nations was aimed at marking a clear line in the sand, one meant to prevent "globalist institutions from infringing on American sovereignty or imposing a radical-left wing agenda on the American People."
Trump also touted his efforts to combat cartel violence along the southern border and in Latin America, saying his decision to designate these groups as foreign terrorist organizations has cleared the way for America's military to kill narco-terrorists across the region.
"The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere, not good people," he said. "They are enemies at war with civilization, using murder, rape, torture, and extortion as instruments of terror. Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled, or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we're doing."
Discussing Russia's war on Ukraine, Trump revealed his administration is currently "working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done."
"It's going to happen," he said, "more quickly than people understand."
Speaking about the hotly watched emergence of the global AI race, Trump—who has dismissed concerns about artificial intelligence safety as "a hoax"—proposed dropping the "AI" name for one that truly communicates both the dangers and possibilities of the technology.
"Super intelligence" will be the new name used by the United States in all communications going forward.
"The use of the word 'artificial' makes intelligence fake," he explained. "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake."
"From this point forward, all of [the] United States' documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, 'super' as opposed to 'artificial.' So it's 'super intelligence.' In other words, welcome to the new world of super intelligence—SI."

sources.news_title: In UN speech, Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened Tuesday to “annihilate” Iran if diplomatic efforts to end his nearly seven-month-old war do not succeed. Speaking to the United Nations General Assembly, he also touted both his peacemaking record and an increasingly belligerent U.S. foreign policy stretching from the Middle East to Venezuela to Greenland.
Trump presented the past year as proof that military force and economic pressure could resolve conflicts that diplomacy had failed to settle.
“As president of the most extraordinary nation in history, I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day,” he declared. “I do not believe in letting problems fester; they only become harder to solve. So while others have talked, I have acted.”
The leading example of this approach, Trump said, was Iran, which, in his telling, has rejected Washington’s diplomatic overtures that had pushed Trump to take military action with Israel in June 2025 and then launch a much larger-scale war beginning at the end of February.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said of the current status of the war. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before (...) Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly?”
Trump has made several similarly dark threats against Iran during the conflict, but they have done little to alter Tehran’s negotiating position, and the two sides appear stuck in a standoff, with some fearing that the operation is doomed to become another American “forever war”.
The president, however, predicted that the two sides will reach an agreement after November’s midterm elections, because “it doesn't make sense for” Iran not to.
“They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election, what they don't realize is that I'm not running,” he added, saying that national security questions, not political considerations will drive his calculus. But the war does seem to be affecting the president’s popularity. A recent poll by CNN shows that opposition to Trump’s approach to the war continues to grow, with only 26% saying that they support the president’s approach, and nearly 80% saying he is not doing enough to bring the war to an end.
Trump blasted the “cowards and traitors” who say that U.S. munitions stockpiles are dwindling to a dangerous extent. The Congressional Budget Office recently found that it could take five years to replenish them.
Elsewhere, Trump said he would “continue to seek and end the disastrous war between Russia and Ukraine,” while threatening to use the “enormous” new tariff authorities granted to him by the Russia sanctions package that passed Congress last week. He also said that he would sign the recently announced deal with Denmark and Greenland that would increase the U.S. military presence in Greenland later Tuesday.
Trump closed his remarks by downplaying the growing worries over artificial intelligence’s threat to humanity, instead presenting the race to “superintelligence” as part of a competition with China.
“Whoever wins superintelligent wins,” he said. “That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way.”

sources.news_title: U.N. speech: Trump says he must make deal with Iran or 'annihilate' the country
Trump's UN takeaways: Threats, diplomacy, and the ICC
sources.text:
President Donald Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly to defend the US-Israeli campaign against Iran while laying out his foreign policy priorities.
Here are the major issues he addressed in a 37-minute speech:
Iran - President Trump warned he could annihilate Iran without a peace deal and predicted one would be reached after US midterm elections on 3 November when the makeup of Congress will be decided.
Ukraine - About Russia's war in Ukraine, he said: "We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," adding, "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand."
Artificial Intelligence - Mr Trump said the US government would use the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and repeated his view that AI safety warnings are a hoax. "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else," he said. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution." He said US law enforcement agencies would rein in the sector if needed.
International Criminal Court - President Trump urged member nations of the International Criminal Court to withdraw - he used the word "resign" - and condemned what he called an "out of control institution" and "an evil group of people." He said the US would not allow military service members to be subject to what he called show trials by an anti-American tribunal.
Drug wars - He said he was "reasserting American power" to make the region safer by taking out cartels, which the US has designated terrorist organisations. "Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release," Mr Trump said, "which is what we're doing."
Venezuela - He characterised his administration's actions in Venezuela as a great victory and a potential warning to others. "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.

Iran says it can reopen the Straight of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eases military pressure and lifts port blockades.
A senior Iranian official delivered the proposal as world leaders gathered in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
The official said Iran transmitted its latest proposal to Washington through intermediaries on September 16, according to Reuters.
The Iranian offer comes after months of war, maritime disruption, sanctions, airstrikes, and mounting pressure on global energy markets.
Washington has maintained a blockade targeting Iranian ports while American forces continue operating throughout the Persian Gulf region.
Iran, meanwhile, has restricted shipping through Hormuz, the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with global markets.
Before the war, roughly one-fifth of globally traded oil and gas moved through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iranian official said Washington must first publicly and formally commit to resolving the confrontation through diplomacy.
“The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the Iranian official said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian traveled to New York Tuesday but is not expected to meet President Donald Trump.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio nevertheless said Washington remains open to talks if negotiations could produce meaningful results.
Rubio said engagement is worthwhile “especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive” for American objectives.
Trump used his United Nations address Tuesday to demand tougher international economic pressure against Tehran from other nations.
“I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” Trump told world leaders.
Trump also said he believes an agreement could emerge after November’s United States midterm elections.
He accused Tehran of delaying negotiations while waiting to see how Republicans perform in those congressional contests.
Trump simultaneously urged Iran to fully reopen Hormuz and return to negotiations aimed at ending the conflict.
The president said he faces “a big decision” over whether diplomacy or overwhelming military force ultimately ends the confrontation.
Iran has also warned that renewed American military operations would trigger retaliation “without limitations and considerations.”
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf separately declared that Tehran would not surrender to American pressure.
“Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces,” Qalibaf said.
Regional governments are watching closely because several Gulf states host major American military installations targeted during the conflict.
Trump planned talks Tuesday with leaders from Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Those governments want commercial shipping restored while remaining wary of arrangements that could expand Iranian influence over regional security.
Qatar has promoted a broader security framework intended to include Iran and Arab Gulf states under mutual guarantees.
Saudi Arabia has simultaneously faced growing pressure from Iran-aligned Houthi forces advancing in Yemen near crucial Red Sea shipping routes.
Those developments have complicated alternatives to Hormuz by threatening transportation around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West Pipeline Tuesday, offering another route for some oil exports toward the Red Sea.
Reuters reported the pipeline had been shut after attacks Riyadh blamed on Iranian-aligned militants operating from Iraq.
The Trump administration has paired military pressure with an economic campaign designed to further isolate Iran from global commerce.
Tehran’s latest proposal does not itself constitute an agreement, and Washington has not announced acceptance of Iran’s conditions.
The current opening therefore represents another diplomatic possibility rather than confirmation that the seven-month conflict is nearing resolution.
For global markets, reopening Hormuz could ease shipping disruptions, although any lasting impact depends on security conditions and implementation.
Iran calls that setting a “golden opportunity,” while Trump continues demanding economic isolation and preserving the possibility of military escalation.

Trump Urges Compete Isolation of Iran, Expects Deal After Election

by Reuters and Algemeiner Staff
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday called for complete economic isolation of Iran, showing no intention to resume talks at the UN General Assembly but saying he believed a deal would be done after the US midterm elections in November.
Iran had earlier hinted at the prospect of reviving negotiations to end their almost seven-month-old conflict, with the presidents of both countries due at the UN in New York.
A senior Iranian official said Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if the US fulfilled Tehran’s demands to ease military pressure and lift an American blockade on Iranian ports, adding that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington via mediators last week.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC’s “Today” show the US was open to speaking with the Iranians, “especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about.”
But in a combative speech to the UN, Trump gave no sign of readiness to compromise.
“I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to. They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
IRAN SEES ‘GOLDEN OPPORTUNITY’ TO REVIVE DIPLOMACY
The senior Iranian official had earlier told Reuters that the US should “announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline.”
“The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the official said.
No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed weeks after it was signed.
In a reminder of Iran‘s firm position so far, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who headed Iran‘s negotiating team at previous talks, said Iran would never surrender: “Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces.”
Trump was due to meet on Tuesday with leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
All are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of global oil and gas shipments before the war, but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
All apart from Oman also host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war.
The biggest of them, Saudi Arabia, has been drawn deeper into the war this month, as Houthi fighters aligned to Iran have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of a Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
There was some relief on oil markets on Tuesday, after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports within hours, albeit at reduced volume, from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s main alternative route for exports to bypass wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, had been shut down after attacks this month that Riyadh blamed on Iranian allies in Iraq. [O/R]
SAUDIS SEEK US SUPPORT AGAINST HOUTHIS
The Houthis have driven back Saudi-supported government forces along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones. The fighters are now pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub Mountains that overlook the Red Sea coast.
The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight. The New York Times reported that Trump called off US strikes against the Houthis on Sunday at the last minute, after troops had already begun loading bombs onto planes.
Asked why Washington had held back from striking the Houthis, Rubio said: “Ultimately, if it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so.
“That said, that is a very dangerous and complex conflict that pre-exists … We have a history with the Houthis as well, and that’s something we don’t want to see impacted either.”
On the table at the Gulf states’ meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said. One source said Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.
“Lasting security cannot be built through repeated cycles of escalations and retaliation, or arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity,” Sheikh Mohammed said.

At UN, Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran but predicts deal after midterms
New York: Donald Trump told world leaders at the United Nations that he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran to end the war, but predicted the two countries would reach a peace deal after the US midterm elections in November.
The US president also rejected what he called a “globalist scheme” to regulate AI – which Australia has joined – and said the US would officially rename artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in a bid to rehabilitate the concept’s image.
Trump said the change would be made on all US government documents regarding AI, and he hoped the world would follow suit. “It sounds much better. It is much better, and it’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don’t – we’re going to find out pretty soon.”
Trump’s speech to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday morning (US time) was less combative than his effort last year, when he lectured the world about the climate change “hoax” and told his global counterparts their countries were “going to hell” thanks to mass migration.
While the president revisited those topics in passing, he focused on opposing AI regulation and defending the war against Iran, which has now lasted nearly seven months.
The war had severely weakened the Islamic theocracy in Tehran, he said, which has lost its entire navy and is suffering from inflation that eclipsed 300 per cent. But a deal to end the conflict collapsed, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps continues to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations? But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election. Because it doesn’t make sense for them not to.
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running. I did that already, and won in a landslide. I’ll be here for 2½ years. The Republican Party is running [in the November election] and I’ll be helping them. But I am not running.”
Trump said he gave no credence to the midterm elections at all when it came to deciding what to do about Iran. “It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
The speech came a day after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese – who is also in New York for UN leaders’ week – joined counterparts from Canada, Europe and elsewhere in calling for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models.
The declaration called for a UN-style international organisation that would set standards and oversee AI use.
Trump’s rejection of this “globalist scheme” reflects his belief that any regime to regulate the sector would cede control to China, the US’ main rival to AI dominance.
“I am not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” he told the UN General Assembly. “Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter or how great or how daunting that challenge may be.”
As he did last year, Trump used the platform to attack elements of the UN itself – including UNESCO and the Human Rights Council – and its “far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats”.
He also lashed out at the International Criminal Court, which he called a “rogue institution” and “an evil group of people”. The ICC – which the US has never been a party to – has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is due to deliver his own address to the UN on Thursday.
When the US president turned his attention to Cuba, branding it “an absolutely failed state” that would soon collapse, the Cuban delegation in the audience walked out of the room.
Trump went on to hold bilateral meetings with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham – their first such encounter – Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as a meeting with members of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
During a brief news conference with Zelensky, Trump said that his special envoy Steve Witkoff, who was in the room, had met with members of the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN. Trump said it was a “very good meeting”.
“It’s to their advantage to make a deal,” he said. “If we can do that, it’s preferable, I guess.” Witkoff declined to elaborate.
Earlier, as he entered the UN building, Trump briefly stopped to speak to reporters, and targeted CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins. CNN was one of three news outlets Trump banned from the White House last week.
“I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump said. “You should not be here. You said you weren’t going to cover me, you shouldn’t be covering me.”
Like other news organisations, CNN received credentials from the UN to cover the General Assembly.

Why babies infected in the womb are ‘more likely to have autism’
Babies could be at a higher risk of autism and intellectual disability if they contract infections such as rubella and herpes in the womb, a new study has suggested.
What you need to know about the study
Researchers from Sweden’s Karolinska Institute analysed health records from 3.7 million people born between 1987 and 2021.
975 of these had been diagnosed with a so-called congenital “torch” infection – a group of parasitic, bacterial and viral diseases.
Children known to have had one of these before birth were around three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism, and seven times more likely to have an intellectual disability.
The researchers also found that those who had been infected, but had neither of these tended to have slightly lower school grades at 16.
Family circumstances not a factor
To check whether genetics or family circumstances might have affected the result, the researchers compared the affected children with siblings who had not contracted a congenital infection, but the associations with autism and intellectual disability remained.
Experts emphasised that infections are very rare, occurring in only around 2.5 per 10,000 births.
The authors said the study strengthened the case for vaccination and other measures that stop infections being passed on to the foetus.
Limitations to the study
The observational study cannot prove that the infections caused autism.
It also relied on clinically diagnosed congenital infections, meaning that milder or symptom-free infections could have been missed.

The rest of the media suspended some coverage of Donald Trump in sympathy, but he has not backed down, setting up his own “Trump TV” live channel.

Why might ban be illegal?
The media companies’ legal argument rests on three grounds: that the ban did not follow “due process” such as allowing notice; that it violates a constitutional right to free speech and that it also violates free speech by denying access to a “non-public forum” (the White House).
Washington DC’s district court judge Timothy Kelly ordered that the defendants file a response the next day, with a hearing set for Wednesday.
What did Trump say?
Trump claimed to have “expected” the lawsuit, and again attacked the media organisations, saying the Oval Office “should be treated with Decorum, Respect, and Dignity, not defiled by Third Rate Clowns”.
But he seemed to anticipate being ruled against in the court, saying “we’ll go for appeal”.
Timothy Kelly previously ruled on a similar case. In 2018, he ordered that a CNN reporter should get his White House press pass back after he was banned following a contentious exchange with the President.
Experts note that because a system has been created that allows journalists access to parts of the White House, courts have placed limits on how access can be withdrawn.
But, an appellate court previously ruled that presidents retain substantial authority over who they allow into limited-access settings.

Major US television outlets agreed to suspend some video coverage of Trump, in a demonstration of solidarity with the banned channels.
No broadcaster covered the ribbon-cutting for the White House’s new helipad, and the President’s remarks were inaudible on a hastily-arranged live stream.

By Michelle Nichols and Daphne Psaledakis
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump on Tuesday called for complete economic isolation of Iran, showing no intention to resume talks at the UN General Assembly but saying he believed a deal would be done after the US midterm elections in November.
Iran had earlier hinted at the prospect of reviving negotiations to end their almost seven-month-old conflict, with the presidents of both countries due at the UN in New York.
A senior Iranian official said Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within seven days if the US fulfilled Tehran’s demands to ease military pressure and lift an American blockade on Iranian ports, adding that Tehran had conveyed its latest proposal to Washington via mediators last week.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC’s “Today” show the US was open to speaking with the Iranians, “especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about.”
But in a combative speech to the UN, Trump gave no sign of readiness to compromise.
“I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to. They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
The senior Iranian official had earlier told Reuters that the US should “announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline.”
“The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the official said.
No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed weeks after it was signed.
In a reminder of Iran’s firm position so far, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who headed Iran’s negotiating team at previous talks, said Iran would never surrender: “Trump must understand that he cannot impose his power on the Iranian people and its armed forces.”
Trump was due to meet on Tuesday with leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
All are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of global oil and gas shipments before the war, but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
All apart from Oman also host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war.
The biggest of them, Saudi Arabia, has been drawn deeper into the war this month, as Houthi fighters aligned to Iran have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of a Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
There was some relief on oil markets on Tuesday, after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports within hours, albeit at reduced volume, from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. O/R
The pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s main alternative route for exports to bypass wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, had been shut down after attacks this month that Riyadh blamed on Iranian allies in Iraq. O/R
The Houthis have driven back Saudi-supported government forces along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones. The fighters are now pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub Mountains that overlook the Red Sea coast.
The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight. The New York Times reported that Trump called off US strikes against the Houthis on Sunday at the last minute, after troops had already begun loading bombs onto planes.
Asked why Washington had held back from striking the Houthis, Rubio said: “Ultimately, if it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so.
“That said, that is a very dangerous and complex conflict that pre-exists … We have a history with the Houthis as well, and that’s something we don’t want to see impacted either.”
On the table at the Gulf states’ meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said. One source said Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.
“Lasting security cannot be built through repeated cycles of escalations and retaliation, or arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity,” Sheikh Mohammed said.

sources.news_title: ‘Drive Them Into Hell’: Trump Makes Wild Threats in Chaotic UN Speech
sources.text:
‘Drive Them Into Hell’: Trump Makes Wild Threats in Chaotic UN Speech
Donald Trump lives in a world of his own. But once a year, at the United Nations General Assembly, he stands in front of representatives from the rest of the planet and tries to justify the violent, chaotic reality he has created.
“While others have talked, I have acted,” Trump said in an early moment in the speech. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace.”
It looked for a while as if bridging this gap between reality and fantasy would be too much for the aging president, who struggled through a roughly 40-minute speech today. But while his performance was lackluster, his rhetoric was not. Speaking directly to a single delegate from Iran, who sat isolated from other members, the president threatened to destroy Iran if his demands were not met.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival, and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
Iran’s delegate stared back at him.
“But I believe we’ll make a deal,” Trump finished. “Right after the election.”
The upcoming midterm elections were very much on Trump’s mind, cropping up several times during his speech. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said of Iran. But his focus drifted to the domestic, too. “What they [Iran] don’t realize is I’m not running,” he said. “The Republican Party is running and I’ll be helping them, but I am not running.”
The subtext to undecided voters was extremely clear: Please don’t let the disastrous, disruptive war stop you from voting red in November. “I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” Trump said. “It doesn’t even enter my mind.”
On one hand, he’s probably telling a version of the truth — given his current polling numbers, it’s hard to imagine Trump making the same decisions he did if he got a do-over.
Like most Trump speeches, his remarks at the UN strayed further from coherence as it went on, devolving into rambling attacks and loose word-association tics referencing various issues of the day. Much of it was loosely aimed at the Democratic Party, claiming that “Christians are being persecuted all over the world,” that the Democrats wanted to let “the worst people” into our country, and repeatedly lamenting the “transgender mutilization of our children.” He claimed to have settled “eight wars,” one up from the tally in last year’s speech, when he claimed he had ended seven. He also tried to rebrand artificial intelligence — AI — as “super intelligence.” “SI — that sounds much better,” Trump said. He made an attempt to justify his brutal actions in Venezuela and around Latin America with several jabs and threats at drug cartels. “The cartels are the ISIS of the western hemisphere,” Trump said. “Not good people!” He spoke about “massive munitions facilities” replacing what the U.S. had shot in Iran.
Trump returned, time and time again, to a line of rhetoric that made it clear who his enemies were. “My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” Trump said. “It’s an absolutely failed state. It’s failing like never before, and it will fall.”
The Cuban delegation immediately walked out of the room. But while delegates at the UN can symbolically withdraw from a speech, no one, it seems, can truly escape the U.S. president. For another two and a half years, it seems, we’re still living in Donald Trump’s world.

sources.news_title: In U.N. speech, Trump threatens to "annihilate" Iran and defends handling of global conflicts
sources.text:
In U.N. speech, Trump threatens to "annihilate" Iran and defends handling of global conflicts
Washington — President Trump defended his handling of conflicts around the world in a speech before the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, saying he could "annihilate" Iran while predicting that its leaders would make a deal to end the war after the U.S. midterm elections.
He framed his approach to foreign policy over his first two years back in office as deploying American power to solve "decades of intractable challenges" that previous U.S. leaders have failed to address.
"I do not believe in letting problems fester. They only become harder to solve. So while others have talked, I have acted," he said.
The roughly 35-minute speech came before Mr. Trump is set to meet with other world leaders on the sidelines of the annual U.N. gathering, including the prime minister of the U.K. and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He is navigating several ongoing international conflicts beyond the war with Iran, which will hit its seven-month mark next week. Mr. Trump is also seeking to close a peace plan for the Gaza Strip between Israel and Hamas, and has struggled to bring Russia's invasion of Ukraine to an end.
In his remarks, the president justified his decision to begin the war with Iran, framing it as an effort to prevent Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. After recounting the run-up to the war and the failed negotiations to end the fighting over the past several months, Mr. Trump said he has "a big decision to make."
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"
"But I believe we'll make a deal, right after the election," he continued. "Because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do on the midterm election. What they don't realize is that I'm not running."
Later Tuesday, Mr. Trump indicated that his son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with the Iranians on the sidelines of UNGA. He said they "had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out."
In his speech, the president said "the United States and Iran will definitely get it done — we will get it done, one way or the other." Mr. Trump also dismissed reports about diminished U.S. munition stockpiles, saying "we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using." The Pentagon's own inspector general said last week that the war in Iran has led to "strategic inventory shortfalls" of munitions.
The president insisted in his speech that he has brought about peace in a way other world leaders could not, while settling years of "unfinished business."
"While others have talked, I have acted," he said. "While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them. While others have talked of courage, America has shown it. While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world."
The president also emphasized the United States' influence in the Western Hemisphere, particularly touting U.S. intervention in Venezuela and procurement of billions of barrels of Venezuelan oil.
"To the victor belong the spoils, you've all heard that," he said. "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States."
The president also touted the new security agreement the U.S. reached with Greenland and Denmark, calling Greenland the "northern frontier of North America." The U.S., which already has a military presence in Greenland, will be able to add new "defense areas" in Greenland, according to the deal. Mr. Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the security agreement later Tuesday. Disputes over Greenland, trade, defense spending and Mr. Trump's push for NATO members to assist with the Iran war have frequently brought him into conflict with Canada and European states over the last year.
The president also continued his tirade against critics of the acceleration of artificial intelligence, while saying he's going to try to rebrand "AI" as "superintelligence" or "SI."
"Every major new technology brings challenges. And superintelligence is no exception," he said. "Yet, the very same people who said we'll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming … and nobody was dead. These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster."
"I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he added, insisting the U.S. will continue to lead the world "safely and responsibly."
Trump at the U.N. and Xi's visit
Mr. Trump is scheduled to meet with a number of leaders on the sidelines of the General Assembly, including U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and various Gulf state leaders. He met with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday. He's also expected to have a pull-aside conversation with acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, about whom Mr. Trump has spoken positively since U.S. forces removed former leader Nicolás Maduro from power.
Mr. Trump is preparing to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a high-stakes state visit. The tenuous U.S.-China relationship is lingering in the background of the General Assembly. American and Chinese negotiators have sought to mend their economic relationship after last year's tit-for-tat trade war, and have discussed opening up communications on the risks posed by artificial intelligence.
The U.S. president has praised Xi in spite of questions about Chinese entities assisting Iran and buying Russian oil. China is the world's largest buyer of Russian crude oil, potentially putting Beijing in the crosshairs of a law signed by Mr. Trump last week threatening heavy tariffs against Russia's largest energy customers.
Mr. Trump dismissed a report by the Wall Street Journal that Chinese entities provided Iran with satellite imagery of a base in Jordan used by U.S. troops before Iran killed three Americans there.
"I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well," Mr. Trump said last week of Xi's conduct during the war with Iran.
The president's movements and meetings at the U.N. won't be nearly as accessible for viewers as in past years.
After the White House banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House, the presidential network pool — consisting of ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — suspended pool coverage of the president. That means there likely won't be television coverage of the president's meetings with foreign leaders. Politico, CNN and MS NOW announced they're suing the Trump administration, citing First Amendment concerns, in an effort to restore access.
Other cameras, however, are covering UNGA as a whole, and captured Mr. Trump on camera as he entered the building.
"You should not be here covering me," the president told a CNN reporter.

UNITED NATIONS — US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he expects Washington to reach a deal with Iran after the November midterm elections, while warning that he faces a “big decision” over whether to pursue an agreement or take further military action against Tehran.
Speaking at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Trump presented the choice in stark terms, saying an agreement could allow Iran to rebuild its country, while the alternative could involve further US military action.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said, before raising the prospect of either reaching an agreement with Tehran or moving to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic.
Trump said he believed an agreement would be reached after the US midterm elections on Nov. 3, arguing that Tehran was waiting to see how Republicans performed at the polls.
“What they don't realize is that I'm not running. I did that already and won in a landslide,” Trump said, adding that the election would not influence his approach toward Iran.
“The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Trump said his administration had opened negotiations with Tehran after he returned to office and offered economic cooperation in return for restrictions on Iran’s nuclear activities and an end to its support for terrorism, but said Tehran rejected the proposal.
He again claimed that US military operations had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear program, and defended his decision to use military force after failed efforts to reach an agreement.
“After giving Iran every chance for a deal, I took action to ensure that neither the United States nor any nation at all would ever have to face such a nightmare,” Trump said.
Trump also made a series of claims about the damage inflicted on Iran’s military capabilities, saying its naval vessels, air force, radar and air defense systems had been destroyed and that its missile and drone manufacturing capacity had been severely degraded.
He further claimed Iran’s economy had been devastated and inflation had risen above 300%.
Trump accused Tehran of violating a ceasefire linked to nuclear discussions by attacking civilian vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
His remarks came as both Washington and Tehran signaled potential openness to renewed diplomacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington was open to talks with Iranian representatives, although no meeting had been scheduled.
Trump also rejected suggestions that the United States was running short of munitions, saying Washington had more than it could “ever possibly even think of using” and was expanding its stockpiles.

sources.news_title: Trump Threatens to ‘Annihilate’ Iran at the U.N.
sources.text:
New York — Before the United Nations General Assembly, a stonefaced Iranian representative among them, President Donald Trump had a question about the enemy in the war he had struggled for months to end.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” Trump said.”Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
It was an ultimatum to Iran on the world’s stage: Make a deal or be destroyed.
It wasn’t a new message. Trump delivered a similar one to his audience — and the world — months earlier on Truth Social, writing, “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”
Trending
It didn’t happen, but the post immediately sparked questions of war crimes and whether the leader of the free world was preparing to commit one. But Tuesday’s comments, delivered from a teleprompter, carried new weight.
In a 38-minute address that saw Trump largely stick to the script and avoid weaving off-the-cuff additions, the president’s main target was the same as it has been since the United States initiated a war with Iran in February. Trump defended the actions he’s taken in the Middle East and other aggressive actions taken across the globe. And alongside the blunt words about the world’s leading state sponsor of terror, Trump informed his allies that America had done what they would not. And instead of admonishing those allies for what Trump said was a lack of action, the president instead asked for their help.
“I call on all nations to join us in enforcing the complete economic isolation of Iran until they stop their attacks on commercial shipping, relinquish their nuclear ambitions and cease their support of terror,” Trump said. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror.”
Trump later confirmed that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours at the summit. U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff took part, Trump said. He described it as a “very good” meeting, but it isn’t clear whether the president participated, given his presence at other events during that time.
His address — and his arrival at the summit — began with domestic issues. Trump’s escalated fight with the press showed up before his remarks, when he told CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins: “You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me. You shouldn’t be covering me.”
He spoke of low crime rates and the drop in crossings at the southern border, economic investments and tourism, before pivoting to the international problems at hand.
Even the political fallout from the Iran war, a seemingly intractable issue that’s weighed heavily on Trump’s approval rating, was a brief subject in the president’s remarks. Trump predicted Iran would strike a deal after the midterm elections “because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” adding that he doesn’t worry about the war’s impact on the midterms.
“It doesn’t even enter my mind,” Trump said. “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Still, a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Sunday found that 34% of respondents approved of the actions against Iran. Republican support for the war also declined, from 73% in March to 60% in the most recent CNN survey.
Between the new threats to end Iran and criticisms of the UN’s Human Rights Council — “What they do is unbelievable” — Trump returned to another usual target: the U.S.’s own backyard.
Trump hailed the Venezuelan operation that captured Nicolás Maduro and the subsequent oil deal that concerned Republican lawmakers. He also dedicated a small but significant portion of his remarks to Cuba and affirmed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in deep negotiations with the island.
“We’ll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep, right at our doorstep,” he added.
When Trump mentioned his administration’s efforts to curb Cuban influence, the representatives of Cuba exited the General Assembly Hall. But their disapproval did not stop Trump’s scripted remarks.
“While others have talked of strength,” Trump said, “I have used it to make America the most powerful in the world.”
But as the address winded down, so did Trump’s dedication to the teleprompter. He debuted his new name for artificial intelligence — “super intelligence” — and wondered whether his influence would be enough to see the change stick. Trump said that all federal documents referencing AI will use the new name.
“We will only encourage super intelligence. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” the president said, while acknowledging there will be some Department of Justice oversight of the technology.
The president delivered his hotly anticipated speech during the morning session of the General Assembly’s first official day. Seated in the hall were Rubio, U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz, chief of staff Susie Wiles and first lady Melania Trump.

President Donald Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend an increasingly interventionist foreign policy, casting himself as a leader willing to use American military, diplomatic and economic power while declaring that the United States would continue to put its own interests first.
“While others have talked, I have acted,” Trump said. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them.”
Much of the speech focused on Iran and the nearly seven-month war that has reshaped the Middle East and disrupted global energy markets. Trump defended his decision to go to war alongside Israel earlier this year and said Tehran had rejected previous efforts to reach an agreement that would prevent it from obtaining nuclear weapons.
Trump said he now faced what he called a “big decision” over whether to reach a deal that would allow Iran to recover or move toward far more destructive military action.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, before saying he nevertheless expected an agreement after the November midterm elections.
Trump said Iranian leaders were waiting to see how Republicans performed in the midterms, though he stressed that he himself was not on the ballot.
“The Republican Party is running, and I’m going to help them,” he said, adding that his principal concern remained ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.
He also rejected reports that concerns over depleted US ammunition and interceptor stocks were constraining his military options, saying the United States possessed large quantities of weapons and was replenishing them rapidly.
Trump called on other countries to join Washington in economically isolating Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping, abandons its nuclear ambitions and stops supporting terrorism.
The war with Iran has complicated Trump’s effort to portray his foreign policy as a series of successful peace interventions. The Wall Street Journal reported that the White House is seeking to present his international record as a collection of tangible wins for Americans ahead of the midterms, even as the wars involving Iran and Ukraine continue to weigh on energy prices and global trade.
Trump invokes Oct. 7 and Gaza deal
Trump also invoked Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, accusing Iran of supporting the terrorists responsible and arguing that Tehran could never be permitted to operate under the protection of a nuclear arsenal.
He said Iran’s supreme leader had celebrated the massacre and described the threat posed by a nuclear-armed Islamic Republic as one the United States could not ignore.
Trump then pointed to Gaza as evidence of what he described as his ability to turn conflict into negotiated outcomes.
He recalled that when he addressed the General Assembly a year earlier, the Gaza war was still underway and hostages remained in Hamas captivity. His administration’s 20-point plan was later endorsed by the UN Security Council, and the Board of Peace was established to oversee the postwar framework. The board says the ceasefire brought the return of all hostages and is now focused on demilitarization, Palestinian civilian administration, reconstruction and humanitarian assistance.
Trump thanked Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries contributing to Gaza, saying their money was reaching areas where humanitarian needs remain acute.
He also praised countries that have committed personnel, police or training to Gaza stabilization efforts, including Indonesia, Morocco, Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan, Egypt and Jordan.
The Board of Peace is scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the General Assembly to review implementation of the Gaza framework and discuss its next priorities.
Ukraine, Greenland and Venezuela next
Trump devoted less time to Russia’s war against Ukraine, saying his administration was continuing efforts to bring the conflict to an end.
His diplomatic agenda after the speech underscored how much unfinished business remains.
He was scheduled to meet separately with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Gulf leaders, with the Iran war expected to feature prominently in the regional discussions. The continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have both contributed to pressure on global energy markets.
Trump was also expected to sign an agreement expanding the US military and commercial presence in Greenland after nearly two years of pressure on Denmark, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Another meeting was set with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, whose government has entered into an arrangement giving the Pentagon a stake in the country’s oil sector. Trump has argued that closer US involvement in Venezuelan energy production will help lower fuel prices at home.
The meeting is politically sensitive because Rodríguez was a senior figure in the government of Nicolás Maduro, who was removed in a US military operation earlier this year. Trump has emphasized cooperation with Rodríguez while moving more slowly on a transition to democratic government, according to the Journal.
Xi summit looms
Trump’s UN appearance also comes on the eve of a three-day state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The two leaders are expected to discuss artificial intelligence, rare earth minerals and Taiwan, among other issues. The Journal reported that Trump, who previously took a more confrontational approach toward Beijing, is now seeking a less adversarial relationship and wants to avoid a deepening economic and military confrontation.
The summit is expected to focus heavily on optics and the broader relationship rather than major new agreements.
Trump’s packed schedule reflects the contrast at the heart of his UN message: he presented himself as a president who has already delivered peace through decisive action, even as some of the largest crises he has confronted remain unresolved.
His Iran policy captures that tension most clearly. Trump threatened Tehran with potentially devastating consequences while simultaneously predicting that diplomacy would ultimately prevail.
“The president is open to a meeting with him or anybody,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian ahead of the speech, while cautioning that Iran’s supreme leader remains the country’s ultimate decision-maker.
For Trump, the message to the General Assembly was that willingness to negotiate and willingness to use force are not contradictory elements of his foreign policy.
“While others have spoken of peace,” he told world leaders, “I have made peace.”

sources.text:
Trump, addressing U.N., threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran if war continues
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon generated applause throughout the chamber.
- The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
NEW YORK — President Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran if it fails to negotiate a deal over its nuclear program, delivering a defensive speech justifying the mission at the United Nations on Tuesday.
His remarks come more than six months into a war that has grown increasingly unpopular at home, with fewer than a third of Americans approving of the president’s handling of the conflict, according to recent polls.
“I have a big decision to make,” he told world leaders gathered at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, with Iranian diplomats in attendance.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy again?
“Do I drive them into hell,” he continued, “with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness?”
The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, increasing inflation and energy prices due to disruptions in commercial shipping traffic through key waterways in the Middle East.
Defense officials say the conflict has also placed a huge burden on U.S. munitions stockpiles, as Iran continues firing ballistic missiles and drones at American assets and bases throughout the region.
But Trump denied that the war has depleted U.S. stocks. “That’s not true,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “We must be equally united in maintaining pressure.”
The rise in global gas prices has sparked protests around the world. But Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon — an issue that for decades united the international community — generated applause throughout the chamber.
The president’s actions stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the U.N. and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Launching the war on Iran in February, Trump projected the campaign would last roughly six weeks, with the stated objective of disabling Iran’s ballistic missile program, its navy and its nuclear infrastructure. He also vowed a day would soon come when the Iranian people could rise up against their government and reclaim their country.
More than six months later, the Islamic Republic stands. Iran’s ballistic missiles continue to test U.S. air defenses across the Middle East, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains depressed, and talks over the future of Iran’s nuclear program have collapsed.
Explaining his decision to start the war, Trump said that he decided not to let the problem of Iran’s nuclear work “fester,” and warned that its ballistic missile program was being designed as a shield to protect its nuclear program from foreign attack.
“Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional ballistic missile shield,” Trump said. “They were the bully of the Middle East, but they’re the bully no more.”
The United States has repeatedly offered a deal with Iran that would open up economic cooperation between the two nations in exchange for an end to their nuclear work, he said.
“They absolutely refused,” he added. “That was a big mistake.”
U.S. and Iranian officials met on the sidelines of the annual general assembly, in a meeting Trump later described as productive.
“Very good meeting,” he told reporters traveling with him in New York. “I can’t imagine why they wouldn’t want to. It’s greatness, potential greatness, or obliteration.”
Latin America on Trump’s mind
When outlining his priorities on the Western Hemisphere, Trump vowed to use “unmatched military might” when necessary if drug cartel activity in other countries poses a threat to the United States.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” Trump said.
Trump said his administration is reasserting its power over regional drug cartels, which he characterized as “the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere.” He said drug cartel members should be “killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release,” and said Mexico was the “epicenter of the cartel violence.”
“Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity,” he said.
In the same remarks, Trump said his administration is seeking a “fundamental change” in Cuba, which he called a “failed state.” He said talks on what comes next for the communist island are being negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“It will fall,” he said, as members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the room.
Also in the room was Delcy Rodríguez, the acting president of Venezuela. She has worked closely with the Trump administration since the U.S. military captured Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face drug trafficking charges.
Rodríguez and Trump were expected to have a “pull aside” meeting, said Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Their encounter is the first time the two leaders met in person since Maduro’s capture.
Because Rodríguez is a holdover from the Maduro government, the meeting has drawn criticism in Venezuela, where many believe Trump is legitimizing her. Earlier this month, those tensions grew when the U.S. government entered an agreement with an oil producer to develop Venezuelan’s vast oil resources, with Rodríguez’s blessing.
The sweeping oil deal raised uncertainty about how entrenched the unelected government may become, more so after Trump said he did not think Venezuela was ready to hold democratic elections yet.
“It’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship and we’re getting along great with the government,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. But he said an election would happen “soon.”
A deal over Greenland
Also Tuesday, after months of threatening to seize Greenland, Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of the Arctic territory and Denmark, one that he lauded as “tremendous for Europe and the United States.”
Details of the deal remained vague upon its signing. But Trump told the General Assembly that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all of the needs” of the Danish territory.
“We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places,” Trump said. “No U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland anymore or make sensitive investments there without our written approval.”
Mette Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, on Tuesday said the accord “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced, though Trump characterized it as more immediate. He told the General Assembly that the United States planned to immediately grow its military presence in the Arctic island.
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” he said. “We will be building two major military bases.”
Frederiksen told Trump on Tuesday that the deal would help protect the United States from foreign adversaries.
“Mr. President, you’ve been very clear you don’t want adversaries to come too close. I fully agree. And with this deal, they are not,” she said. “We are making sure that they will not be allowed to get any control or significant influence in Greenland.”
Wilner reported from New York and Ceballos from Washington.

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he insisted to applause in the chamber.

“We are settling years of unfinished business. And we’re doing it well. There is no better example of a danger that was allowed to gather strength at the world’s peril than the number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said.

They added: “The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy.”
The comments come as Washington and Tehran remain locked in a tense stand-off, with Mr Trump using his UN address to raise the prospect of both a renewed deal with Iran and further military action if diplomacy fails.
